deep.lede: Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus, who forgives his sins before healing him. All three Synoptics tell the story with heavy shared wording, which makes it a classic laboratory for the Synoptic problem. It has small editorial changes in every verse and several minor agreements.

sections.heading: Mud roof or tiled roof?
sections.body:
Mark's description fits a Galilean house with a roof of beams and packed earth: they {mk 2:4 ἀπεστέγασαν τὴν στέγην ὅπου ἦν καὶ ἐξορύξαντες} (“unroofed the roof where he was, and having **dug through** it”). Luke adapts the scene to the kind of house his readers would picture: {lk 5:19 διὰ τῶν κεράμων καθῆκαν αὐτὸν} (“they let him down **through the tiles**”). Some see this as a historian's mistake, others as a thoughtful translation, much as a modern preacher might say “through the ceiling”. Matthew drops the roof altogether.

The bed changes too. Mark's {mk 2:4 κράβαττον} was a colloquial word for a poor man's pallet, which literary writers avoided. Matthew and Luke both replace it with forms of *klinē* (“bed”): Matthew's {mt 9:2 ἐπὶ κλίνης} and Luke's {lk 5:18 ἐπὶ κλίνης}. This is a minor agreement, and a typical case of the later Gospels polishing Mark's Greek.

sections.heading: Forgiveness first
sections.body:
The surprise in all three is that Jesus answers the friends' faith with forgiveness, not healing: {mk 2:5 Τέκνον ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι} (“child, your sins are forgiven”). The scribes object: {mk 2:7 τίς δύναται ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός} (“who can forgive sins but God alone?”). Jesus answers with a riddle: {mk 2:9 τί ἐστιν εὐκοπώτερον} (“which is easier?”). Saying “your sins are forgiven” is easy to claim and impossible to check; “get up and walk” can be tested. The healing that follows makes the invisible claim visible.

Matthew adds {mt 9:2 Θάρσει} (“take heart”), and Luke changes “child” to {lk 5:20 Ἄνθρωπε} (“man”).

sections.heading: Three endings, one agreement
sections.body:
Matthew and Luke both report that the man {mt 9:7 ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ} / {lk 5:25 ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ} (“went away to his house”). Mark has Jesus command this ({mk 2:11 ὕπαγε εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου}) but narrates only that he {mk 2:12 ἐξῆλθεν ἔμπροσθεν πάντων} (“went out before them all”). It is a small minor agreement, but one of several in this unit.

The crowd's reactions differ. Mark: {mk 2:12 Οὕτως οὐδέποτε εἴδομεν} (“we have never seen anything like this”). Luke: {lk 5:26 Εἴδομεν παράδοξα σήμερον} (“we have seen paradoxical things today”), the source of the English word “paradox”. Matthew, uniquely, has the crowd glorify God {mt 9:8 τὸν δόντα ἐξουσίαν τοιαύτην τοῖς ἀνθρώποις} (“who had given such authority **to human beings**”). The plural seems to extend the authority to forgive to Matthew's church.

deep.lede: A man asks Jesus how to gain eternal life, is told to sell everything, and goes away grieving. “The rich young ruler” is a composite: only Matthew calls him young, only Luke calls him a ruler, and all three agree he was rich. The opening exchange also contains one of the best-known theological edits in the Gospels.

sections.heading: “Why do you call me good?”
sections.body:
In Mark the man kneels and says {mk 10:17 Διδάσκαλε ἀγαθέ} (“Good Teacher”), and Jesus replies {mk 10:18 Τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός} (“why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone”). Luke keeps this word for word ({lk 18:19 Τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν}).

Matthew moves the adjective. The man asks {mt 19:16 Διδάσκαλε τί ἀγαθὸν ποιήσω} (“Teacher, what **good thing** must I do?”), and Jesus says {mt 19:17 Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ} (“why do you ask me **about the good**?”). The change removes any implication that Jesus disclaimed being good. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for Markan priority. It is easy to see why Matthew would soften Mark's version, and very hard to see why Mark would make Matthew's version more awkward.

sections.heading: Love, and the one thing lacking
sections.body:
Only Mark says that Jesus {mk 10:21 ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτὸν} (“looked at him and loved him”). It is the only time in the Synoptics that Jesus is said to love a specific individual, and both Matthew and Luke leave it out. Then: {mk 10:21 Ἕν σε ὑστερεῖ} (“you lack one thing”).

Matthew moves the lack into the man's own mouth: {mt 19:20 τί ἔτι ὑστερῶ} (“what do I still lack?”). Only Matthew calls him a {mt 19:20 νεανίσκος} (“young man”), and adds a condition: {mt 19:21 Εἰ θέλεις τέλειος εἶναι} (“if you wish to be **perfect**”). Later Christian ethics built on this phrase a two-level distinction between commandments for everyone and “counsels of perfection” for monks, a reading many interpreters think goes beyond Matthew's intention.

sections.heading: The camel and the needle
sections.body:
The man leaves grieving, {mk 10:22 ἦν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά} (“for he had many possessions”). Matthew copies the phrase exactly ({mt 19:22 ἦν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά}); Luke heightens it: {lk 18:23 ἦν γὰρ πλούσιος σφόδρα} (“for he was **extremely** rich”). Luke also calls him {lk 18:18 ἄρχων} (“a ruler”).

Jesus' image of a {mk 10:25 κάμηλον διὰ τῆς τρυμαλιᾶς τῆς ῥαφίδος} (“camel through the eye of a needle”) has attracted softening explanations: a supposed “Needle Gate” in Jerusalem (there is no evidence for one), or a misreading of *kamēlos* (camel) as *kamilos* (rope), a reading found in some late manuscripts. Rabbinic texts use an elephant through a needle's eye as a proverb for the impossible. The exaggeration is deliberate, and the answer is {mk 10:27 πάντα γὰρ δυνατὰ παρὰ τῷ θεῷ} (“for all things are possible with God”).

deep.lede: Jesus returns to his hometown and is rejected. Mark and Matthew place this midway through the ministry as a short scene. Luke places it at the very beginning (traditional readers take it as an earlier, separate visit) and expands it into a programmatic sermon that ends with an attempt to kill him. Together the versions also show a careful reworking of an embarrassing line.

sections.heading: Carpenter, or carpenter's son?
sections.body:
Mark's townspeople ask {mk 6:3 οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τέκτων ὁ υἱὸς τῆς Μαρίας} (“isn't this **the carpenter**, the son of Mary?”). It is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus himself is called a *tektōn*, a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Matthew changes it to {mt 13:55 ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός} (“the carpenter's **son**”). Luke has {lk 4:22 υἱός ἐστιν Ἰωσὴφ οὗτος} (“isn't this Joseph's son?”), and John {jn 6:42 Ἰησοῦς ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωσήφ}.

Why change it? Early critics of Christianity, such as Celsus, mocked a manual laborer as savior, and Origen replied that no canonical Gospel calls Jesus a carpenter. Some manuscripts of Mark do indeed read “the son of the carpenter”. Calling a man “son of Mary” rather than of his father was also unusual, and some scholars think it is a deliberate slur on his birth.

sections.heading: “He could not”
sections.body: Mark says something theologically startling: {mk 6:5 οὐκ ἐδύνατο ἐκεῖ ποιῆσαι οὐδεμίαν δύναμιν} (“he **could not** do any mighty work there”), apart from healing a few sick people, and {mk 6:6 ἐθαύμαζεν διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν} (“he was amazed at their unbelief”). Matthew rewrites it: {mt 13:58 οὐκ ἐποίησεν ἐκεῖ δυνάμεις πολλὰς} (“he **did not** do many mighty works there”). Inability becomes choice, and “not any” becomes “not many”. It is a textbook example of the redaction criticism that underpins the theory of Markan priority.

sections.heading: Luke's inaugural sermon
sections.body:
Luke turns the scene into Jesus' first public act. In the synagogue {lk 4:16 κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ} (“as was his custom”), he reads Isaiah 61: {lk 4:18 Πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ ἐμέ} (“the Spirit of the Lord is upon me”), to bring good news to the poor and release to captives. Then he announces {lk 4:21 Σήμερον πεπλήρωται ἡ γραφὴ αὕτη ἐν τοῖς ὠσὶν ὑμῶν} (“today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing”). The rest of Luke–Acts follows this program.

The mood turns when Jesus cites Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners. The crowd tries to throw him {lk 4:29 ἕως ὀφρύος τοῦ ὄρους} (“to the brow of the hill”). The proverb that all four Gospels share is phrased differently in each. Luke's is {lk 4:24 οὐδεὶς προφήτης δεκτός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ πατρίδι αὐτοῦ} (“no prophet is **acceptable** in his hometown”), a pun on the “acceptable year of the Lord” he has just read. John's is {jn 4:44 προφήτης ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ πατρίδι τιμὴν οὐκ ἔχει}. Its context in John is puzzling, since Jesus is welcomed in Galilee, and commentators still debate which “homeland” John means.

deep.lede: Jesus sleeps in a boat during a storm, the terrified disciples wake him, and he silences the wind. All three Synoptics tell it, and the disciples' words to Jesus change in a way that shows how each evangelist treated them.

sections.heading: “Don't you care?”
sections.body:
In Mark the disciples rebuke Jesus: {mk 4:38 Διδάσκαλε οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα} (“Teacher, don't you care that we are perishing?”). Matthew turns the complaint into a prayer, {mt 8:25 Κύριε σῶσον ἀπολλύμεθα} (“**Lord, save**, we are perishing”), words that his church could use in worship. Luke softens it to a cry of alarm: {lk 8:24 Ἐπιστάτα ἐπιστάτα ἀπολλύμεθα} (“Master, Master, we are perishing”). Only the verb, “we are perishing”, survives all three edits, and it is the likely core of the tradition.

Mark's sleeping Jesus is also a vivid detail: {mk 4:38 ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ ἐπὶ τὸ προσκεφάλαιον καθεύδων} (“in the stern, asleep on **the** cushion”). Both Matthew and Luke drop the cushion, the kind of eyewitness-sounding detail that Mark often has and the others often omit.

sections.heading: Silencing the sea
sections.body: Jesus speaks to the storm as if it were a demon. Mark: {mk 4:39 ἐπετίμησεν τῷ ἀνέμῳ καὶ εἶπεν τῇ θαλάσσῃ Σιώπα πεφίμωσο} (“he **rebuked** the wind and said to the sea, ‘Silence! Be muzzled!’”). The verb *phimoō* (“muzzle”) is the one Jesus used to silence an unclean spirit (1:25). In the Hebrew Bible the sea is a symbol of chaos that only God controls, and Psalm 107:29 says he “made the storm be still”. The disciples' final question, {mk 4:41 Τίς ἄρα οὗτός ἐστιν} (“who then is this?”), has only one biblical answer.

sections.heading: No faith, or little faith?
sections.body:
The rebuke of the disciples changes in each Gospel. Mark: {mk 4:40 οὔπω ἔχετε πίστιν} (“do you **still have no** faith?”). Matthew: {mt 8:26 ὀλιγόπιστοι} (“you of **little** faith”), and he places the rebuke **before** the miracle, so that Jesus talks to his disciples while still lying in the storm. Luke: {lk 8:25 Ποῦ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν} (“**where** is your faith?”), which implies that they have faith but failed to use it.

Mark's disciples in general come off poorly, and Matthew and Luke consistently rehabilitate them. Scholars debate why Mark was so hard on them. Proposals range from a polemic against Jerusalem leaders to a pastoral message that failure is not final.

deep.lede: That Jesus was baptized by John is among the best-attested facts about his life, partly because it was awkward. Why would the sinless Messiah undergo a baptism of repentance, administered by someone presented as his inferior? The four Gospels can be read as four increasingly careful responses to that embarrassment. Traditional readers see complementary emphases instead: each evangelist brings out a different side of why the sinless one was baptized.

sections.heading: Mark: the plain fact
sections.body: Mark says it directly: Jesus {mk 1:9 ἐβαπτίσθη εἰς τὸν Ἰορδάνην ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου} (“was baptized in the Jordan by John”). Coming up from the water, **he** sees the heavens {mk 1:10 σχιζομένους} (“being torn open”), and the voice speaks to him alone: {mk 1:11 Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός} (“**You** are my beloved Son”). In Mark the experience is private; nothing suggests anyone else saw or heard it. The words blend Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1.

sections.heading: Matthew: John objects
sections.body:
Matthew alone adds a dialogue. John tries to prevent it: {mt 3:14 Ἐγὼ χρείαν ἔχω ὑπὸ σοῦ βαπτισθῆναι} (“I need to be baptized by you”). Jesus answers {mt 3:15 οὕτως γὰρ πρέπον ἐστὶν ἡμῖν πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην} (“it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”). These are Jesus' first words in Matthew, and they bring in Matthew's key term, righteousness.

The voice becomes public: {mt 3:17 Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός} (“**This** is my beloved Son”). It is an announcement to bystanders, not a word to Jesus. The heavens are {mt 3:16 ἠνεῴχθησαν} (“opened”) rather than torn, a gentler verb that Luke also uses ({lk 3:21 ἀνεῳχθῆναι τὸν οὐρανὸν}). That shared verb is a minor agreement.

sections.heading: Luke: the baptizer goes missing
sections.body: Luke's narrative is subtle. He describes John's imprisonment **before** the baptism (3:19–20), then says only {lk 3:21 Ἰησοῦ βαπτισθέντος καὶ προσευχομένου} (“when Jesus had been baptized and was praying”). He never says who baptized him. The emphasis moves to prayer, a constant theme in Luke, and to physical reality: the Spirit came {lk 3:22 σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡς περιστερὰν} (“in **bodily** form, like a dove”). Luke then gives Jesus' age, {lk 3:23 ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα} (“about thirty years old”), a detail found nowhere else.

sections.heading: John: no baptism at all
sections.body: The Fourth Gospel never narrates the baptism. John the Baptist only testifies to what he saw: {jn 1:32 Τεθέαμαι τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον ὡς περιστερὰν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐπ αὐτόν} (“I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it **remained** on him”). John's favorite verb, *menō* (“remain”, “abide”), makes the Spirit a lasting presence. The Baptist's conclusion has a significant variant: SBLGNT prints {jn 1:34 ὁ ἐκλεκτὸς τοῦ θεοῦ} (“the **Chosen One** of God”), supported by some early manuscripts, while most manuscripts and translations read “the Son of God”. A scribe might well have changed “Chosen One” to the familiar title, but not the reverse.

deep.lede: A vineyard owner sends servants and finally his son to collect his rent, and the tenants kill them all. It is the most openly allegorical of the Synoptic parables, and the Jerusalem leaders recognize at once that it is aimed at them. Small differences in the order of events show the evangelists reading Jesus' death into the story.

sections.heading: Isaiah's vineyard
sections.body: Mark's opening echoes Isaiah 5, the Song of the Vineyard, in which Israel is God's vineyard: {mk 12:1 Ἀμπελῶνα ἄνθρωπος ἐφύτευσεν καὶ περιέθηκεν φραγμὸν καὶ ὤρυξεν ὑπολήνιον καὶ ᾠκοδόμησεν πύργον} (“a man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress, and built a tower”). Every listener would recognize the source. But in Jesus' version the vineyard isn't at fault, the **tenants** are. The target has moved from the people to their leaders, and Matthew says explicitly that {mt 21:45 ἔγνωσαν ὅτι περὶ αὐτῶν λέγει} (“they knew he was speaking about them”).

sections.heading: Killed, then thrown out, or thrown out, then killed?
sections.body:
Mark's order is {mk 12:8 ἀπέκτειναν αὐτόν καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος} (“they killed him and threw him out of the vineyard”), leaving the body unburied, which was a final insult. Matthew and Luke both reverse it: {mt 21:39 ἐξέβαλον ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος καὶ ἀπέκτειναν} and {lk 20:15 ἐκβαλόντες αὐτὸν ἔξω τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος ἀπέκτειναν} (“they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him”).

Why? Jesus was crucified **outside** the city walls (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12 makes a point of it). Both later evangelists seem to have adjusted the parable to match the Passion. It is a minor agreement that both theories can explain as independent editing toward the same, obvious goal.

sections.heading: The beloved son
sections.body: Mark's owner has {mk 12:6 ἕνα εἶχεν υἱὸν ἀγαπητόν} (“one beloved son”), the same phrase as the heavenly voice at the baptism. Luke gives the owner an inner monologue, {lk 20:13 Τί ποιήσω} (“what shall I do?”), and a hesitant hope: {lk 20:13 ἴσως τοῦτον ἐντραπήσονται} (“**perhaps** they will respect him”). The tenants' logic, {mk 12:7 Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ κληρονόμος} (“this is the heir”), may reflect a real legal situation: property with no heir could be claimed by those in possession.

sections.heading: Who gets the vineyard?
sections.body:
In Matthew the audience pronounces its own sentence: {mt 21:41 Κακοὺς κακῶς ἀπολέσει αὐτούς} (“he will put those wretches to a wretched death”), a Greek wordplay. Matthew then adds a verse found only in his Gospel: {mt 21:43 ἀρθήσεται ἀφ ὑμῶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς} (“the kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a people producing its fruits”). The verse has a long history of supersessionist readings, in which the Church replaces Israel. Many scholars argue that in context it targets Jerusalem's leaders, not the Jewish people.

In Luke the audience recoils: {lk 20:16 Μὴ γένοιτο} (“may it never be!”). All three close with Psalm 118:22, {mk 12:10 Λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες} (“the stone the builders rejected”). There is a pun in Hebrew, where *ben* (son) and *eben* (stone) sound alike.

deep.lede: “Let anyone among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone.” The story of the woman caught in adultery is among the most loved in the Gospels, and it almost certainly wasn't part of John's Gospel originally. It is a story that circulated for centuries looking for a home in the Gospels, and its history is part of what the site's textual-variants layer is meant to show.

sections.heading: A story without a home
sections.body:
The passage (John 7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John, including P66, P75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. No Greek church father comments on it for the first thousand years. Where it does appear, it moves around: after John 7:36, after 7:44, at the end of John, and in one group of manuscripts after Luke 21:38. Its vocabulary also fits Luke better than John. The opening, {jn 7:53 Καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ} (“and each went to his own house”), reads like the end of some other story.

Yet the story is old. The third-century *Didascalia Apostolorum* refers to it, and the historian Eusebius mentions a similar story of a woman accused of many sins, which he knew from the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Most scholars conclude that it is an early, perhaps authentic, tradition about Jesus that was added to the canon late.

sections.heading: The trap
sections.body: The scribes and Pharisees bring {jn 8:3 γυναῖκα ἐν μοιχείᾳ καταλήφθεισαν} (“a woman caught in adultery”) and cite Moses. The law required both partners to be put to death (Leviticus 20:10), and the man's absence is conspicuous. Their purpose is stated: {jn 8:6 ἵνα ἔχωσιν κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ} (“so that they might have grounds to accuse him”). If Jesus says “stone her”, he contradicts his reputation for mercy and claims a power of execution that Rome reserved for itself. If he says “release her”, he sets aside the law of Moses. It is the same kind of trap as the question about taxes to Caesar, which the Synoptics place in the same Temple setting.

sections.heading: Writing in the dust
sections.body: Jesus' response is to stoop and write: {jn 8:6 κάτω κύψας τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν} (“bending down, he wrote with his finger on the ground”). It is the only time the Gospels show Jesus writing, and they don't say what he wrote. Suggestions include the accusers' own sins (an idea found in some later manuscripts that add “the sins of each of them”), Jeremiah 17:13 (“those who turn away from you will be written in the earth”), or simply that he was declining to engage. The phrase “with his finger” may echo the tablets of the law, written “by the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18).

sections.heading: Neither do I condemn you
sections.body: The famous saying, {jn 8:7 Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὸν λίθον βαλέτω} (“let the one without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her”), doesn't abolish the law; it questions the authority of the judges. The accusers leave one by one, “beginning with the elders”. The ending holds mercy and demand together: {jn 8:11 Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κρίνω πορεύου καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε} (“neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more”). Some scholars think it was this mercy, not doubts about its history, that kept the story out of early Gospel texts. In a church that imposed strict penance for adultery, the story may have seemed too lenient.
